title: 156. Binary Tree Upside Down
description: Given the root of a binary tree, turn the tree upside down and return the new root.
steps: The original left child becomes the new root.
The original root becomes the new right child.
The original right child becomes the new left child.
note: The mentioned steps are done level by level. It is guaranteed that every right node has a sibling (a left node with the same parent) and has no children.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree will be in the range [0, 10].
Every right node in the tree has a sibling (a left node that shares the same parent).
Every right node in the tree has no children.

title: 157. Read N Characters Given Read4
description: Given a file and assume that you can only read the file using a given method read4, implement a method to read n characters.
steps: The API read4 reads four consecutive characters from file, then writes those characters into the buffer array buf4.
The return value is the number of actual characters read.
Note that read4() has its own file pointer, much like FILE *fp in C.
By using the read4 method, implement the method read that reads n characters from file and stores it in the buffer array buf.
You cannot manipulate the file directly. The file is only accessible via read4, not read.
The read function will only be called once per test case.
You may assume the destination buffer buf has enough space for storing n characters.
note: buf[] is a destination, not a source. You will need to write the results to buf[].
constraints: file consists of English letters and digits.

title: 158. Read N Characters Given read4 II - Call Multiple Times
description: Given a file and assume that you can only read the file using a given method read4, implement a method read to read n characters. Your method read may be called multiple times.
steps: The API read4 reads four consecutive characters from file, then writes those characters into the buffer array buf4.
The return value is the number of actual characters read.
Note that read4() has its own file pointer, much like FILE *fp in C.
By using the read4 method, implement the method read that reads n characters from file and stores it in the buffer array buf.
You cannot manipulate the file directly. The file is only accessible via read4, not read.
The read function may be called multiple times.
Class-level variables should be reset between test cases.
You may assume the destination buffer buf has enough space for storing n characters.
It is guaranteed that in a given test case the same buffer buf is used by multiple read calls.
note: buf[] is a destination, not a source. You will need to write the results to buf[].

examples.explanation: First read returns 1 character ("a"), second read returns 2 characters ("bc"), third read returns 0 as end of file is reached.
First read returns 3 characters ("abc"), second read returns 0 as end of file is reached.

constraints: file consists of English letters and digits.

title: 159. Longest Substring with At Most Two Distinct Characters
description: Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring that contains at most two distinct characters.
steps: Use a sliding window to track a valid substring with at most two distinct characters.
Maintain a hashmap or dictionary to count character frequencies.
Shrink the window from the left whenever the number of distinct characters exceeds two.
Track the maximum length seen throughout the process.
note: This is a common sliding window problem involving character frequency tracking.

examples.explanation: The substring is "ece" which its length is 3.
The substring is "aabbb" which its length is 5.

title: 161. One Edit Distance
description: Given two strings s and t, return true if they are both one edit distance apart, otherwise return false.
steps: Check if the strings differ in length by more than 1 — if so, return false immediately.
Compare both strings character by character.
If a mismatch is found, consider the three possibilities: insert, delete, or replace a character.
Only one such operation must be allowed for the result to be true.
After checking the first difference, ensure the rest of the strings match accordingly.
note: A string s is said to be one edit distance apart from a string t if you can insert, delete, or replace exactly one character in s to make it equal to t.

examples.explanation: We can insert 'c' into s to get t.
We cannot get t from s by only one step.

constraints: s and t consist of lowercase letters, uppercase letters, and digits.

title: 163. Missing Ranges
description: You are given an inclusive range [lower, upper] and a sorted unique integer array nums, where all elements are within the inclusive range. A number x is considered missing if x is in the range [lower, upper] and x is not in nums. Return the shortest sorted list of ranges that exactly covers all the missing numbers.
steps: Initialize a pointer to track the previous number (start with lower - 1).
Iterate through nums plus one extra step to handle the upper bound.
For each number, if the current number is more than the previous + 1, there's a missing range.
Format missing ranges as [start, end] pairs and collect them.
Return the list of all such missing ranges.
note: Ensure that no element in nums is included in the output. Each missing number should be part of exactly one range.

examples.explanation: There are no missing ranges since there are no missing numbers.

constraints: All the values of nums are unique.

title: 170. Two Sum III - Data structure design
description: Design a data structure that accepts a stream of integers and checks if it has a pair of integers that sum up to a particular value.
steps: Initialize an internal data structure to store the numbers (e.g., a HashMap or array).
On calling add(number), store the number in the data structure.
On calling find(value), check if any two stored numbers add up to the given value.
If such a pair exists, return true; otherwise, return false.
note: This is an implementation problem requiring efficient insert and lookup to support up to 10^4 operations.

examples.explanation:
TwoSum twoSum = new TwoSum();
twoSum.add(1);   // [1]
twoSum.add(3);   // [1,3]
twoSum.add(5);   // [1,3,5]
twoSum.find(4);  // 1 + 3 = 4 → true
twoSum.find(7);  // No such pair → false

constraints: At most 10^4 calls will be made to add and find.

title: 186. Reverse Words in a String II
description: Given a character array s, reverse the order of the words. A word is defined as a sequence of non-space characters. The words are separated by a single space.
steps: Reverse the entire character array.
Then reverse each word individually to restore word characters in correct order.
Perform all operations in-place without using extra space.
note: You must solve the problem in-place without allocating extra space.
constraints: s[i] is an English letter (uppercase or lowercase), digit, or space ' '.
There is at least one word in s.
s does not contain leading or trailing spaces.
All the words in s are guaranteed to be separated by a single space.

title: 243. Shortest Word Distance
description: Given an array of strings wordsDict and two different strings that already exist in the array word1 and word2, return the shortest distance between these two words in the list.
steps: Iterate through the wordsDict array while tracking the most recent indices of word1 and word2.
Every time both indices are set, update the shortest distance if the current one is smaller.
Return the minimum distance found.
note: The two words are guaranteed to be different and exist in the list.
constraints: wordsDict[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
word1 and word2 are in wordsDict.

title: 244. Shortest Word Distance II
description: Design a data structure that will be initialized with a string array, and then it should answer queries of the shortest distance between two different strings from the array.
steps: Store indices of each word during initialization for fast lookup.
When queried, retrieve both word indices lists and compute the shortest distance using a two-pointer approach.
note: Multiple queries will be made after the object is initialized, so optimize for repeated lookups.
constraints: wordsDict[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
word1 and word2 are in wordsDict.
At most 5000 calls will be made to shortest.

title: 245. Shortest Word Distance III
description: Given an array of strings wordsDict and two strings word1 and word2 (which may be the same), return the shortest distance between the occurrence of these two words in the list. Note that if word1 and word2 are the same, they represent two individual words in the list.
steps: Iterate over the wordsDict array once while tracking the most recent indices of word1 and word2.
If word1 and word2 are different, update the shortest distance whenever both indices have been seen.
If word1 and word2 are the same, track previous occurrence and current occurrence to calculate the distance.
Return the minimum distance found.
note: This problem allows word1 and word2 to be the same word, which requires careful handling.
constraints: wordsDict[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
word1 and word2 are in wordsDict.

title: 246. Strobogrammatic Number
description: Given a string num which represents an integer, return true if num is a strobogrammatic number. A strobogrammatic number is a number that looks the same when rotated 180 degrees (looked at upside down).
steps: Create a mapping of valid strobogrammatic digit pairs (e.g., '0'->'0', '1'->'1', '6'->'9', '8'->'8', '9'->'6').
Use two pointers, start and end, at the beginning and end of the string respectively.
While start <= end, check if num[start] and num[end] form a valid strobogrammatic pair.
If any pair is invalid, return false.
If all pairs are valid, return true.
constraints: num does not contain any leading zeros except for zero itself.

title: 247. Strobogrammatic Number II
description: Given an integer n, return all the strobogrammatic numbers that are of length n. A strobogrammatic number is a number that looks the same when rotated 180 degrees (looked at upside down). You may return the answer in any order.

title: 248. Strobogrammatic Number III
description: Given two strings low and high that represent two integers low and high where low <= high, return the number of strobogrammatic numbers in the range [low, high]. A strobogrammatic number is a number that looks the same when rotated 180 degrees (looked at upside down).
constraints: low and high consist of only digits.
low and high do not contain any leading zeros except for zero itself.

title: 249. Group Shifted Strings
description: We can shift a string by shifting each of its letters to its successive letter. For example, "abc" can be shifted to "bcd". We can keep shifting the string to form a sequence like "abc" -> "bcd" -> ... -> "xyz". Given an array of strings, group all strings that belong to the same shifting sequence. You may return the answer in any order.
constraints: strings[i] consists of lowercase English letters.

title: 250. Count Univalue Subtrees
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the number of uni-value subtrees. A uni-value subtree means all nodes of the subtree have the same value.

examples.explanation: The tree has 4 uni-value subtrees.
Empty tree has no subtrees.
The tree has 6 uni-value subtrees.

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree will be in the range [0, 1000].

title: 251. Flatten 2D Vector
description: Design an iterator to flatten a 2D vector. It should support the next and hasNext operations.
steps: Vector2D(int[][] vec) initializes the object with the 2D vector vec.
next() returns the next element from the 2D vector and moves the pointer one step forward. You may assume that all the calls to next are valid.
hasNext() returns true if there are still some elements in the vector, and false otherwise.

examples.explanation:
Vector2D vector2D = new Vector2D([[1, 2], [3], [4]]);
vector2D.next();    // return 1
vector2D.next();    // return 2
vector2D.next();    // return 3
vector2D.hasNext(); // return True
vector2D.hasNext(); // return True
vector2D.next();    // return 4
vector2D.hasNext(); // return False

constraints: At most 10^5 calls will be made to next and hasNext.
note: Follow up: As an added challenge, try to code it using only iterators in C++ or iterators in Java.

title: 252. Meeting Rooms
description: Given an array of meeting time intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], determine if a person could attend all meetings.

title: 253. Meeting Rooms II
description: Given an array of meeting time intervals intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], return the minimum number of conference rooms required.

title: 254. Factor Combinations
description: Numbers can be regarded as the product of their factors. Given an integer n, return all possible combinations of its factors. You may return the answer in any order. Note that the factors should be in the range [2, n - 1].

title: 255. Verify Preorder Sequence in Binary Search Tree
description: Given an array of unique integers preorder, return true if it is the correct preorder traversal sequence of a binary search tree.
constraints: All the elements of preorder are unique.
note: Follow up: Could you do it using only constant space complexity?

title: 256. Paint House
description: There is a row of n houses, where each house can be painted one of three colors: red, blue, or green. The cost of painting each house with a certain color is different. You have to paint all the houses such that no two adjacent houses have the same color. The cost of painting each house with a certain color is represented by an n x 3 cost matrix costs.
steps: For example, costs[0][0] is the cost of painting house 0 with red, costs[1][2] is the cost of painting house 1 with green, and so on.
You must paint all houses so that no two adjacent houses have the same color.
Return the minimum total cost to paint all houses.

examples.explanation: Paint house 0 into blue, house 1 into green, and house 2 into blue. Total cost = 2 + 5 + 3 = 10.

title: 259. 3Sum Smaller
description: Given an array of n integers nums and an integer target, find the number of index triplets i, j, k with 0 <= i < j < k < n that satisfy the condition nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] < target.

examples.explanation: There are two triplets which sums are less than 2: [-2,0,1] and [-2,0,3]

title: 261. Graph Valid Tree
description: You have a graph of n nodes labeled from 0 to n - 1. You are given an integer n and a list of edges where edges[i] = [a_i, b_i] indicates that there is an undirected edge between nodes a_i and b_i in the graph. Return true if the edges of the given graph make up a valid tree, and false otherwise.
constraints: There are no self-loops or repeated edges.

title: 265. Paint House II
description: There are a row of n houses, each house can be painted with one of the k colors. The cost of painting each house with a certain color is different. You have to paint all the houses such that no two adjacent houses have the same color. The cost of painting each house with a certain color is represented by an n x k cost matrix costs.
steps: For example, costs[0][0] is the cost of painting house 0 with color 0; costs[1][2] is the cost of painting house 1 with color 2, and so on.
Return the minimum cost to paint all houses.

examples.explanation: Paint house 0 into color 0, paint house 1 into color 2. Minimum cost: 1 + 4 = 5; Or paint house 0 into color 2, paint house 1 into color 0. Minimum cost: 3 + 2 = 5.

note: Follow up: Could you solve it in O(nk) runtime?

title: 266. Palindrome Permutation
description: Given a string s, return true if a permutation of the string could form a palindrome and false otherwise.
constraints: s consists of only lowercase English letters.

title: 267. Palindrome Permutation II
description: Given a string s, return all the palindromic permutations (without duplicates) of it. You may return the answer in any order. If s has no palindromic permutation, return an empty list.
constraints: s consists of only lowercase English letters.

title: 269. Alien Dictionary
description: There is a new alien language that uses the English alphabet. However, the order among the letters is unknown to you. You are given a list of strings words from the alien language's dictionary, where the strings in words are sorted lexicographically by the rules of this new language. Return a string of the unique letters in the new alien language sorted in lexicographically increasing order by the new language's rules. If there is no solution, return an empty string "". If there are multiple solutions, return any of them.

examples.explanation: The order is invalid, so return "".

constraints: words[i] consists of only lowercase English letters.

title: 270. Closest Binary Search Tree Value
description: Given the root of a binary search tree and a target value, return the value in the BST that is closest to the target. If there are multiple answers, return the smallest.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4].

title: 271. Encode and Decode Strings
description: Design an algorithm to encode a list of strings to a string. The encoded string is then sent over the network and decoded back to the original list of strings.
steps: Machine 1 (sender) has the function encode(vector<string> strs) which returns an encoded string.
Machine 2 (receiver) has the function decode(string s) which returns the original list of strings.
The encoded string from Machine 1 is sent to Machine 2, which decodes it back to the original list.
You must implement both encode and decode methods.
You cannot use serialize methods like eval.
note: The encoded string should be able to handle any possible characters in the strings, including special characters.
constraints: strs[i] contains any possible characters out of 256 valid ASCII characters.
follow_up: Could you write a generalized algorithm to work on any possible set of characters?

title: 272. Closest Binary Search Tree Value II
description: Given the root of a binary search tree, a target value, and an integer k, return the k values in the BST that are closest to the target. You may return the answer in any order.
note: You are guaranteed to have only one unique set of k values in the BST that are closest to the target.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is n.
follow_up: Assume that the BST is balanced. Could you solve it in less than O(n) runtime (where n = total nodes)?

title: 276. Paint Fence
description:
You are painting a fence of n posts with k different colors. You must paint the posts following these rules:
- Every post must be painted exactly one color.
- There cannot be three or more consecutive posts with the same color.

examples.explanation: All the possibilities are shown. Note that painting all the posts red or all the posts green is invalid because there cannot be three posts in a row with the same color.

constraints: The testcases are generated such that the answer is in the range [0, 2^31 - 1] for the given n and k.

title: 277. Find the Celebrity
description:
Suppose you are at a party with n people labeled from 0 to n - 1 and among them, there may exist one celebrity. The definition of a celebrity is that all the other n - 1 people know the celebrity, but the celebrity does not know any of them.

You want to find out who the celebrity is or verify that there is not one. You can only ask questions like: "Hi, A. Do you know B?" to get information whether A knows B. Implement a function int findCelebrity(n). There will be exactly one celebrity if they are at the party.

Return the celebrity's label if there is a celebrity at the party. If there is no celebrity, return -1.

examples.explanation: There are three persons labeled with 0, 1 and 2. graph[i][j] = 1 means person i knows person j, otherwise graph[i][j] = 0 means person i does not know person j. The celebrity is the person labeled as 1 because both 0 and 2 know him but 1 does not know anybody.
There is no celebrity.

note: If the maximum number of allowed calls to the API knows is 3 * n, try to find a solution without exceeding the maximum number of calls.

title: 280. Wiggle Sort
description: Given an integer array nums, reorder it such that nums[0] <= nums[1] >= nums[2] <= nums[3]... You may assume the input array always has a valid answer.

examples.explanation: [1,6,2,5,3,4] is also accepted.

constraints: It is guaranteed that there will be an answer for the given input nums.
note: Follow up: Could you solve the problem in O(n) time complexity?

title: 281. Zigzag Iterator
description: Given two vectors of integers v1 and v2, implement an iterator to return their elements alternately.
steps: Initialize the iterator with two vectors v1 and v2.
Use hasNext() to check if any elements remain.
Use next() to return the current element and advance the iterator.
Elements are returned alternately from v1 and v2 until all are exhausted.

examples.explanation: By calling next repeatedly until hasNext returns false, the order of elements returned by next should be: [1,3,2,4,5,6].

note: Follow up: What if you are given k vectors? How well can your code be extended to such cases? The "Zigzag" order is ambiguous for k > 2, and can be replaced with a "Cyclic" order instead.

title: 285. Inorder Successor in BST
description: Given the root of a binary search tree and a node p in it, return the in-order successor of that node in the BST. If the given node has no in-order successor in the tree, return null.
steps: Understand that the successor of a node p is the node with the smallest key greater than p.val.
If p has a right child, the successor is the leftmost node in p's right subtree.
Otherwise, start from the root and search for the successor by comparing values.
Track the potential successor when moving left in the tree.
Return the tracked successor or null if none is found.

examples.explanation: 1's in-order successor node is 2.
There is no in-order successor of the current node, so the answer is null.

constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4].
All Nodes will have unique values.

title: 286. Walls and Gates
description: You are given an m x n grid rooms initialized with three possible values: -1 (a wall or obstacle), 0 (a gate), and INF (2147483647, representing an empty room). Fill each empty room with the distance to its nearest gate. If it is impossible to reach a gate, leave the room as INF.
steps: Identify all gates (cells with value 0) and add them to a queue.
Perform a Breadth-First Search (BFS) starting from all gates simultaneously.
For each step in the BFS, update neighboring empty rooms with the distance from the gate.
Skip walls and already updated cells with shorter distances.

title: 288. Unique Word Abbreviation
description: Design a class that checks whether a given word's abbreviation is unique in a dictionary. The abbreviation is formed by the first letter, the number of letters between the first and last letter, and the last letter. Words with only two letters are abbreviated as themselves.
steps: Create a map to store abbreviations as keys and a set of words having that abbreviation as values.
To check uniqueness, generate the abbreviation of the word.
If the abbreviation is not in the map, it's unique.
If the abbreviation maps only to the same word, it's also unique.
Otherwise, it's not unique.

examples.explanation:
Abbreviations:
- deer, dear -> d2r (not unique)
- cart -> c2t (unique)
- cane, cake -> c2e (not unique)
- make -> m2e (unique)
- cake is in the dictionary and no other word shares its abbreviation

constraints: dictionary[i] consists of lowercase English letters
word consists of lowercase English letters
At most 5000 calls will be made to isUnique

title: 291. Word Pattern II
description: Given a pattern and a string s, determine if s matches the pattern with a bijective mapping from characters in the pattern to non-empty substrings in s. Bijective mapping means each character maps to one unique substring and vice versa.
steps: Use backtracking to try all possible mappings from pattern characters to substrings of s.
Keep two dictionaries: one from pattern to string, and another from string to pattern (to ensure bijection).
Recursively check each character in the pattern against substrings in s.
If a character already has a mapping, verify it matches the current portion of s.
If not, try all valid new mappings and continue recursion.
Backtrack if no valid mapping is found.

examples.explanation: a -> "red", b -> "blue"
a -> "asd"

constraints: pattern and s consist only of lowercase English letters

title: 293. Flip Game
description: You're playing a flip game where you can flip any two consecutive '++' into '--'. Given a string currentState, return all possible states after one valid move.
steps: Iterate over the input string from index 0 to length - 2.
Check if the current and next characters are both '+'.
If so, flip them to '--' and append the new string to the result list.
Continue checking the rest of the string.
Return the list of all such possible states.

title: 294. Flip Game II
description: You're playing a Flip Game with a friend. Given a string `currentState` of '+' and '-', you can flip any two consecutive '++' to '--'. Players take turns and the one who cannot move loses. Return true if the starting player can guarantee a win, false otherwise.
approach: Use backtracking with memoization (DP) to try every valid move. If any move leaves the opponent in a losing position, then the current player can win.
steps: Define a recursive function that tries all valid moves.
For each move that flips '++' to '--', call the function recursively on the new state.
If any of these recursive calls return false (i.e., the opponent loses), then return true.
Use memoization to cache results for repeated states.
If no winning move is found, return false.

examples.explanation: Flip the middle '++' to '+--+', which leads to a win for the starting player.

follow_up: Use memoization to avoid recomputation. Runtime complexity is approximately O(2^N), but with memoization it is significantly reduced, depending on the number of unique states.

title: 296. Best Meeting Point
description: Given a 2D binary grid where 1s represent friends' homes, return the minimal total Manhattan distance to a meeting point. Manhattan distance is calculated as |x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|.
approach: To minimize the total travel distance, we should find the median of all the row and column indices where people live. The Manhattan distance is minimized at the median in 1D. So, we collect all row indices and all column indices where grid[i][j] == 1, sort them, and compute distances to their medians.
steps: Collect the row indices of all 1s (homes) in the grid.
Collect the column indices of all 1s (homes).
Sort both lists.
Compute the total distance as the sum of absolute differences to the median of the row list and the median of the column list.

examples.explanation: Friends at (0,0), (0,4), and (2,2) meet at (0,2) or (2,2), both giving total distance 6.

constraints: There are at least two friends in the grid

title: 298. Binary Tree Longest Consecutive Sequence
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the length of the longest path where the values increase by one consecutively. The path must go downwards (parent to child), not upwards.
approach: Use DFS (depth-first search) traversal. At each node, compare its value with the parent. If it's parent + 1, increment the current sequence length. Otherwise, reset it to 1. Keep track of the maximum length found globally.
steps: Initialize a global variable `maxLen` to keep track of the longest path.
Define a recursive helper function that takes the current node, the previous value, and current length.
If current node value == previous + 1, increase length; else reset it to 1.
Update `maxLen` with the current length if it's greater.
Recurse left and right.
Return `maxLen` after DFS completes.

examples.explanation: The path 3→4→5 is the longest consecutive path.
The path 2→3 is the longest consecutive path.

title: 302. Smallest Rectangle Enclosing Black Pixels
description: Given a binary matrix where '1' represents black pixels (connected in one region), and given the coordinates of one black pixel (x, y), find the area of the smallest axis-aligned rectangle that encloses all black pixels. The algorithm must run faster than O(mn).
approach: Use binary search to find the topmost, bottommost, leftmost, and rightmost rows/columns that contain a black pixel. This avoids scanning the entire matrix. The total number of binary search operations is O(m log n + n log m).
steps: Binary search rows to find the top and bottom boundaries of the black pixel region.
Binary search columns to find the left and right boundaries.
Check within each row or column if there's any '1' to determine whether to expand/shrink the search space.
Calculate area using (bottom - top) * (right - left).

examples.explanation: The smallest rectangle enclosing all black pixels spans from (0,1) to (2,2), area = 3*2 = 6.

constraints: Black pixels form a single connected region
Algorithm must run in less than O(mn) time

title: 305. Number of Islands II
description: You are given a 2D binary grid initialized with water. For each land addition at position (r, c), return the number of islands after that operation. An island is a group of adjacent land cells (horizontally or vertically connected).
approach: Use Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union - DSU) to efficiently track connected land components. For each addition, connect the new land with its adjacent lands if they exist and are already part of an island.
steps: Initialize a Union-Find structure with m * n nodes (each cell).
Maintain a set to track which cells are currently land.
For each land addition at (r, c):
- If the cell is already land, skip.
- Otherwise, mark it as land and increment the island count.
- Check the 4 neighboring cells; if any is land and not in the same set, union them and decrement the island count.
Record the current island count.

examples.explanation: Each new land creates or merges islands based on neighbors.

follow_up: You can solve it in O(k log(mn)) time using Union-Find with path compression and union by rank.

title: 308. Range Sum Query 2D - Mutable
description: Design a 2D matrix structure that supports efficient updates and range sum queries over a subrectangle. You need to implement both update and sumRegion operations.

class_design.int sumRegion(int row1, int col1, int ro: Returns the sum of elements in the subrectangle from (row1, col1) to (row2, col2).

approach: Use a 2D Binary Indexed Tree (Fenwick Tree) to achieve O(log m * log n) time for both update and sumRegion. Store a copy of the original matrix to track value differences during updates.
steps: Maintain a 2D BIT of size (m+1)x(n+1).
On update(row, col, val): calculate the delta between the new value and the current value, and update the BIT.
On sumRegion: compute the prefix sum from (0,0) to (r,c) using BIT and apply inclusion-exclusion to get the desired subregion sum.

title: 311. Sparse Matrix Multiplication
description: Given two sparse matrices mat1 (m x k) and mat2 (k x n), compute their product mat1 x mat2 efficiently by leveraging sparsity.
key_points: Multiplication can be optimized by skipping zero elements to avoid unnecessary computations.
approach: For each non-zero element in mat1, multiply it by the corresponding non-zero elements in mat2 and accumulate the results for the resulting matrix. Use nested loops but skip zeros to improve performance.
steps: Initialize a result matrix of size m x n with all zeros.
For each row i in mat1:
For each column j in mat1 row i:
If mat1[i][j] != 0:
For each column l in mat2:
If mat2[j][l] != 0:
result[i][l] += mat1[i][j] * mat2[j][l]
